name: Arapaho
confidence_why: The reference grammar of Cowell & Moss 2008 describes Arapaho word prominence as a lexically specified, contrastive pitch accent and Salzmann 1956 as two contrastive pitch levels, but Bogomolets 2020 and 2023, on fieldwork and acoustic measurements, reanalyse the same prominence as lexical stress confined to a right-edge three-syllable window with default penultimate stress plus a separate falling tone, and Weber et al. 2023, co-authored by Cowell and Bogomolets, still call Arapaho's prosodic structure uncertain.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Arapaho with an empty rule, so nothing to agree or disagree with. Salzmann supplies the earliest phonemic statement: two-level pitch on every vowel with loudness riding on high pitch, no positional stress rule. The open_url (WALS refdb record) is only a bibliographic entry and the DOI target at journals.uchicago.edu could not be reached by automated download; the article was read from the open archive.org full text of IJAL 22(1).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Salzmann gives no word-stress placement rule. He analyzes Northern Arapaho as having two contrastive level-pitch prosodemes (high vs. low) on every vowel, marked with an acute accent, and states that the high-pitch prosodeme is additionally correlated with greater loudness. Pitch is lexically distributed (several high-pitched vowels can occur in one word, e.g. hínííwého? 'his grandmother', nih?óóθoo 'spider'), so prominence is not assigned by a positional rule. Each register has phonetic variants (he transcribes six levels), with lower variants in contour-final and extra-low in phrase-final position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; no stress degrees are recognized, only two pitch registers with phonetic sub-variants (p. 52).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 52: 'occasionally a given morpheme—besides having automatic alternant shapes as to pitch—may freely vary as to pitch from speaker to speaker or even with one speaker at different times'; contour-final and phrase-final lowering of either register; possible pitch-marking errors where 1949 field notes lacked wire recordings (fn. 8, p. 51).
new_statements.identity_note: Salzmann 1956 explicitly describes Northern Arapaho as spoken on the Wind River Indian Reservation, Wyoming (§1.0, p. 49), and uses 'Arapaho' for that dialect throughout. The Bogomolets works held by the project also treat Northern Arapaho (Wyoming). No description of Southern (Oklahoma) Arapaho was opened.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tonal' record and the existing Salzmann 1956 statement (two prosodemes, high vs low pitch, acute = high): Goddard uses Salzmann's forms and marking, confirms the pitch contrast is phonemic in modern Arapaho, and adds (a) an accentual framing (the acute-marked high pitch is 'the accent', level in Arapaho vs falling in Atsina), (b) the observation that accent placement in nouns is largely predictable from Proto-Arapaho-Atsina word shape (initial in old disyllables; second-vowel accent from shortening, compensatory lengthening or contraction), with exceptions, and (c) the explicit statement that as of 1974 the synchronic accentual system was undescribed and verb-…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Goddard (a diachronic study whose Arapaho forms come from Salzmann 1956-1967, acute = Salzmann's high pitch) treats Arapaho prosody as an 'accent' realised as pitch. Synchronically the accent is contrastive: 'prosodic contrasts were phonemic' in modern Arapaho (p. 111, with the pair I float / I am hanging differing only in accent placement), and fn. 7 (p. 104) says 'A complete lexicon of Arapaho would have to mark accent on verb stems.; stem accentuation cannot be indicated in this paper, however, because the accentual system has not yet been described.' Diachronically he expects placement to be 'almost wholly predictable from the Proto-Arapaho-Atsina shapes': old disyllables accent the first vowel (ébes 'beaver'); disyllables accented on the second vowel are shortened old trisyllables (wonót), or have a second vowel lengthened by compensatory lengthening under rule (14), which 'tends to draw the accent' (betééč 'brain'), or arise from contraction (hiθóóx). Rule (14), p. 110: on such lengthened vowels 'in Arapaho the pitch is generally marked as level, while in Atsina it seems regularly to be falling', and 'an accent appears to have been engendered when an A-A *ʔ dropped after a vowel sequence'. §4.2 opens by saying the rules that 'would predict the prosodic contours of the attested forms' have not been worked out and cannot be until 'the synchronic rules governing these phenomena in the two dialects have been worked out'. No fixed stress position is stated; no statement that stress is absent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Forms are cited with more than one acute (e.g. betééč, onóuθíne-nóó), i.e. multiple high-pitched/accented vowels per word as in Salzmann's notation, but Goddard does not rank them.
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are a few exceptions to these patterns, such as neck (under [19])' (p. 115); verb-stem accent must be lexically marked and is omitted throughout because 'the accentual system has not yet been described' (fn. 7, p. 104); Arapaho level vs Atsina falling pitch on rule-(14) lengthened vowels (p. 110).
new_statements.identity_note: Goddard 1974 covers Arapaho proper (Northern Arapaho as recorded by Salzmann) and Atsina (Gros Ventre, from Taylor) as two dialects of one language, with passing mention of Besawunena, Nawathinehena and Ha'anahawunena; the Arapaho statements quoted are about Arapaho proper. The Atsina-specific remark (falling rather than level pitch on rule-14 lengthened vowels) belongs to Gros Ventre (atsi1235), not arap1274.

new_statements.quote: p. 39: "Any accent-bearing unit can bear accent in Arapaho, i.e. there are no restrictions on where accent can fall. [...] Perhaps, pitch-accent in Arapaho could be best described as morpho-lexical; it is a property of a word, but this property is dependent on morphological and morphemic information." p. 1: "This language has only one level tone – high tone, contrasted with neutral tone, no-tone syllables. Arapaho can hardly be called a prototypical stress language either. The system exhibits regular violations of the principles of culminativity and obligatoriness of stress allowing for up to five accented syllables per word as well as for unaccented words (mostly categorical)."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Arapaho (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing_statements, so nothing is contradicted; this work supplies the placement statement (no positional rule; lexical/morpho-lexical accent, multiple accents per word, unaccented words possible) and adds the instrumental finding that the cues are F0+amplitude on short vowels and duration on long vowels. It explicitly disputes the traditional TYPE label 'pitch accent language' (Salzmann, Goddard 2001, Cowell 2008) on phonetic grounds, not the placement facts.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Arapaho accent (traditionally called pitch accent: high vs. no tone, with a conditioned falling allotone on long vowels/diphthongs) has no fixed position: any syllable can carry it, placement is lexical/morpho-lexical (underlying accent on morphemes, intermorphemic shifts at the word level, grammatical shifts in plurals, locatives, iteratives, participles, citing Cowell 2008), a word may carry up to five accents and some words are unaccented. The thesis's instrumental result (one male speaker, 120 isolated words) is that accent is not cued by F0 alone: short accented vowels have significantly higher F0 and amplitude, long accented vowels are cued by longer duration, and unaccented mid vowels reduce in quality; the author concludes Arapaho 'can hardly be called a pitch accent language' and phonetically 'functions more like a stress-accent system', while phonologically violating culminativity and obligatoriness.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not analysed: fn. 1 (p. 1) and fn. 23 (p. 71) state that whether multiple accents in a word differ as primary vs. secondary is unknown and out of scope; the thesis only notes (quoting Cowell 2008: 90, p. 41) that initial pitch-accents and some final pitch-accents on short vowels have lowered prominence, and that word-level rules redistribute accents to avoid adjacent accented syllables (Cowell 2008: 85, p. 39).
new_statements.exceptions: Unaccented words exist ('mostly categorical', p. 1); up to five accented syllables per word; falling contour (high-to-normal) occurs only on long vowels and diphthongs and is treated as a conditioned allophone (rules on pp. 40-41), no rising contour; final unaccented syllables closed by glottal stop can sound prominent (Cowell 2008: 90, quoted p. 41); native speakers are reported to be poor at marking accents (Cowell, quoted p. 39).
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis treats Arapaho as one language (Northern Arapaho speaker recorded at CU Boulder for the Arapaho Database Project; one adult male speaker, isolated words); no dialect distinction is drawn. Atsina/Gros Ventre is not covered.

readall_conflicts: Only Salzmann 1956 among the listed works could be opened. It frames Arapaho prominence as two contrastive level-pitch prosodemes on every vowel (a tone analysis) with high pitch correlated with greater loudness, and gives no placement rule. The later material already held by the project in our check folder (Bogomolets 2020 PhD; Bogomolets 2023 'Accent and tone in Arapaho', pp. 219-221) reanalyzes the same Northern Arapaho system as a lexical accent (stress) system, with accent position unpredictable within the morpheme, rightmost accent winning in competition, a trisyllabic right-edge window, default penultimate stress, multiple primary stresses per word, and a separate lexical tone system. The two are not contradictory on the facts (both mark the same acute-accented vowels, both say position is lexical), but differ in analytic type: Salzmann = tone/pitch registers, Bogomolets = lexical accent plus independent tone. Bogomolets 2014 (MA thesis) could not be downloaded (not reachable by automated download), so its content is unverified here. No substantive conflict. The catalog records Arapaho as 'tonal' on the strength of Salzmann 1956 (every vowel carries high or low level pitch, acute = high). Goddard 1974, working from Salzmann's own transcriptions, calls the same acute-marked high pitch 'accent'/'accentuation' and speaks of 'the pitch' of accented vowels, i.e. a pitch accent framing of the same contrast; he confirms it is phonemic synchronically (p. 111) and says the syn…

sources.quote: p.42: 'although the position of stress in a given morpheme is unpredictable (i.e. Arapaho is a lexical stress language), the distribution of stresses within a morphological word can be explained with a highly constrained Directional Accent account, comprising of (i) a three-syllable window at the right edge of a morphological word, (ii) underlying accent specification for each of the morphemes within a wordform, (iii) default penultimate accent, and (iv) a Directional accent competition resolution whereby the right-most lexical accent wins.' Presupposes a H vs unmarked lexical tone analysis of Arapaho pitch accent.
